strengths: The task is useful and clearly motivated: combine a reference image with a clothing-change description to retrieve the same person. ITCPR contributes 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery drawn from three datasets, with manually annotated relative captions and additional positive-label verification.

The reported improvements are substantial. With ViT-L/14, Word4Per achieves 45.913% Rank-1 and 55.630% mAP, exceeding the strongest reported non-Word4Per baseline by 10.536 and 11.546 percentage points, respectively.

The two-stage framework is technically coherent and practical. It uses existing person image–text supervision without training on composed-query triplets, and the lightweight inversion network permits reuse of frozen encoders and precomputed gallery features.

The experiments examine two backbones, visual versus textual supervision, training-data quantity, network architecture, prompts, and ensembles. The equations, framework diagrams, hyperparameters, and runtime measurements provide useful implementation guidance.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. Table I and Section V-B indicate that Pic2Word and SEARLE retain inversion networks trained with the original CLIP parameters, including when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. This creates a potentially mismatched representation space, whereas Word4Per learns its mapper specifically for the adapted encoders. Retraining competing mappers with the same encoders and person data is necessary to establish methodological superiority. This is a principal reason for rejection.

The evaluation lacks a clearly independent model-selection protocol. ITCPR is explicitly designated exclusively for testing, yet architecture, hidden width, prompts, and other configurations are selected using its results. No separate validation set or alternative selection procedure is described. This risks optimistic estimates despite the absence of triplet-based gradient training and materially weakens the zero-shot evaluation.

Methodological originality is modest. Mapping image features into pseudo-word tokens closely follows Pic2Word and SEARLE, while the encoder fine-tuning uses established person-retrieval losses. Text-supervised inversion and the person-specific benchmark are useful contributions, but the paper needs stronger controlled evidence to establish the added capability beyond combining these existing techniques.

Benchmark reliability and coverage remain insufficiently characterized. Section IV-A verifies top-k neighbors returned by an unspecified visual encoder, without reporting k or auditing positives outside that candidate pool; this does not establish the claimed elimination of false negatives. Annotation agreement and results broken down by source dataset or modification type are also absent, limiting confidence in the benchmark's labels and generality.

The mechanistic interpretation exceeds the evidence. Figure 9 visualizes the shared frozen visual encoder, so it cannot establish how different TINet supervision changes background dependence. Figure 10 offers only a few examples. Controlled background perturbations and identity-versus-clothing tests would better support the proposed explanation. Repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are also needed to interpret small improvements from combined losses and prompt choices.

Some implementation details are ambiguous or inconsistent. Section V-C selects Table V's row 4 as the final prompt, whereas Section III-C specifies the row-5 template. Section III-D is unclear about whether ensembles average pseudo-word embeddings or encoded composed queries. These distinctions affect reproduction and should be resolved in an explicit final configuration.

For the intended release of identity-linked person imagery and the stated public-security applications, the manuscript does not document source-data redistribution permissions or discuss consent, privacy, and surveillance misuse. These are relevant research-ethics documentation gaps, although the manuscript alone does not establish misconduct.
